# Tidy Data {#sec-tidy}

::: {.callout-note}
## What this chapter covers
The tidy data principles that the rest of Part III builds on: what tidy data is,
why it matters, the five ways real data fails to be tidy, and a map of the
tidyverse functions that fix each problem.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup-tidy
#| include: false
library(webexercises)
```

## What tidy data is

Tidy data is a way of organising a dataset that makes it easier to analyse and
visualise. It is the organising idea behind the whole tidyverse, and it comes
down to three rules:

1. **Each variable forms a column.** Each column contains all values for a
   single variable.
2. **Each observation forms a row.** Each row contains all values for a single
   observation.
3. **Each value has its own cell.**

```{r}
#| label: fig-tidydata
#| echo: false
#| out.width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: |
#|   Tidy data, illustrated by Allison Horst.
#| fig-alt: |
#|   Cartoon showing tidy data: variables in columns, observations in rows.
knitr::include_graphics("images/tidy_data.jpeg")
```

### Why it matters

- **Manipulation becomes predictable.** Every tidyverse function expects tidy
  data, so filtering, transforming and summarising work the same way every time.
- **Readability.** Anyone who knows the rules can understand the layout of your
  data without you explaining it.
- **Compatibility.** Tidy data flows into `ggplot2`, into modelling functions,
  and into table packages without reshaping at each step.

```{r}
#| label: fig-nontidy
#| echo: false
#| out.width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: |
#|   Non-tidy data, illustrated by Allison Horst.
#| fig-alt: |
#|   Cartoon showing messy, non-tidy data.
knitr::include_graphics("images/non_tidy_data.jpeg")
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Tidy is about shape, clean is about content
These two words get used interchangeably and they should not be. **Tidy** means
the layout follows the three rules above. **Clean** means the values are
correct: no typos, no impossible measurements, consistent units, right types.

A dataset can be immaculately tidy and full of errors, or perfectly accurate and
completely untidy. You need both. Reshaping is covered in @sec-pivot; cleaning
in @sec-cleaning.
:::

## The five common problems

According to [Hadley Wickham](https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v059i10/),
there are five problems you will meet repeatedly:

1. **Column headers are values, not variable names.**
   `2019`, `2020`, `2021` as column names; the variable is *year*.
   → `pivot_longer()`
2. **Multiple variables are stored in one column.**
   A column called `sp_m_014` holding diagnosis, sex and age group.
   → `pivot_longer()` with `names_sep`, or `separate_wider_delim()`
3. **Variables are stored in both rows and columns.**
   → `pivot_longer()` then `pivot_wider()`
4. **Multiple types of observational unit in the same table.**
   Patient characteristics repeated on every visit row.
   → `select()` and `distinct()` to split into two tables
5. **A single observational unit spread across multiple tables.**
   Exposure in one register, outcome in another.
   → the joins in @sec-joins

Problems 1 to 3 are solved by pivoting and separating; 4 and 5 by splitting and
joining.

## A map of the functions

The essential tidyverse data-manipulation functions, grouped by what they do:

| What you want to do | Functions | Chapter |
|---------------------|-----------|---------|
| Work with columns | `mutate()`, `select()`, `rename()`, `relocate()` | @sec-dplyr |
| Work with rows | `filter()`, `slice()`, `arrange()`, `distinct()` | @sec-dplyr |
| Group and aggregate | `summarise()`, `group_by()`, `.by`, `count()` | @sec-dplyr |
| Reshape | `pivot_longer()`, `pivot_wider()`, `separate_wider_delim()` | @sec-pivot |
| Combine datasets | `left_join()`, `inner_join()`, `anti_join()` | @sec-joins |
| Handle text | `str_squish()`, `str_replace()`, `str_detect()` | @sec-strings-factors |
| Handle categories | `fct_relevel()`, `fct_recode()`, `fct_reorder()` | @sec-strings-factors |
| Handle missing data | `drop_na()`, `replace_na()`, `is.na()`, `na_if()` | @sec-cleaning |
| Get an overview | `glimpse()`, `count()`, `skimr::skim()` | @sec-eda |

## A worked example

The `palmerpenguins` dataset is already tidy, which makes it a good reference
point.

```{r}
#| label: tidy-penguins
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)

glimpse(penguins)
```

Each row is one penguin. Each column is one property of that penguin. Each cell
holds one value. All three rules hold.

Here is the same information stored untidily — one row per measurement:

```{r}
#| label: tidy-untidy-example
penguins_untidy <- penguins |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  mutate(penguin_id = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g),
    names_to = "measurement",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  select(penguin_id, species, measurement, value)

penguins_untidy
```

This layout is not *wrong* — it is exactly what `ggplot2` wants for a faceted
plot of all four measurements. But it is untidy in the strict sense: the
`value` column holds four different variables measured in different units, so
`mean(value)` is meaningless.

```{r}
#| label: tidy-back
penguins_untidy |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measurement, values_from = value)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Tidy is a means, not an end
The three rules are a default that makes most tasks easier, not a law. Long
format for plotting, wide format for a reader — you will move between them
constantly, and that is normal. What matters is knowing which shape you are in
and why.
:::

## Missing data in a tidy dataset

There are two kinds of missing value, and they need different treatment:

- **Explicitly missing**: an `NA` in a cell. The observation exists; the value
  is unknown.
- **Implicitly missing**: the row is simply not there. A participant who missed
  a visit has no row for that visit at all.

```{r}
#| label: tidy-implicit
visits <- tribble(
  ~id, ~visit, ~score,
  1, "baseline", 12,
  1, "followup", 15,
  2, "baseline", 9,
  3, "baseline", 14,
  3, "followup", NA
)

visits
```

Participant 2 has no follow-up row at all; participant 3 has a row with `NA`.
`complete()` makes the implicit missingness explicit:

```{r}
#| label: tidy-complete
visits |>
  complete(id, visit)
```

Now both participants show a missing follow-up, and a count of missing values
gives the right answer.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Implicit missingness silently changes your denominator
`summarise(n = n(), .by = visit)` on the original data reports two follow-up
observations, which looks like complete data for those two people. After
`complete()`, it reports three, one of which is missing. Only the second is an
honest description of the study.

This is one of the most common ways a longitudinal analysis quietly reports the
wrong sample size.
:::

## Coding best practices

::: {.callout-note}
## The habits that make analysis reproducible
- **Everything you do to your data is documented in code.** No manual edits.
- **You can retrace every step** from raw data to result.
- **Follow a consistent style**, such as the
  [tidyverse style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org/): `snake_case`, `<-` for
  assignment, one verb per line.
- **Use version control** ([Git](https://git-scm.com/)) to track changes and
  collaborate. Commit early, commit often, and write messages that say *why*.
- **Comment the why, not the what.** `# drop participants without a baseline
  measurement` is useful; `# filter rows` is not.
- **Set a seed** before anything random.
- **Use `here::here()`** for file paths, never `setwd()`.
:::

### Avoid `.RData`, prefer `.rds`

- `.RData` saves many objects at once and preserves their attributes, but it is
  not human-readable and you cannot tell what is inside without loading it — at
  which point it silently overwrites objects in your session.
- `.rds` saves a single object, is explicit about what you are loading
  (`data <- readRDS(...)`), and does not touch anything else.
- For anything that needs to be readable outside R, use CSV.

Related: turn **off** "restore .RData at startup" and set "save workspace on
exit" to **Never** in RStudio's global options. A script that only works because
of something left over in your environment is not reproducible, and this setting
is how you find out.

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
**Check yourself**

In tidy data, each row is
`r mcq(c("a variable", answer = "an observation", "a value", "a dataset"))`

A dataset can be tidy and still contain errors. `r torf(TRUE)`

Column names like `2019`, `2020`, `2021` are an example of which problem?
`r mcq(c(answer = "Column headers are values, not variable names", "Multiple variables in one column", "One unit across multiple tables", "Implicit missingness"))`

Which function makes implicitly missing rows explicit?
`r mcq(c("drop_na()", "replace_na()", answer = "complete()", "fill()"))`
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Exercise 1: is this tidy?

For each dataset, say whether it is tidy. If not, say which rule is broken and
which function would fix it.

```{r}
#| label: ex1-tidy-data
# a)
a <- tribble(
  ~country, ~`1999`, ~`2000`,
  "Sweden", 745, 2666,
  "Norway", 37737, 80488
)

# b)
b <- tribble(
  ~country, ~year, ~rate,
  "Sweden", 1999, "0.7/19",
  "Sweden", 2000, "2.7/20",
  "Norway", 1999, "37/172"
)

# c)
c_data <- tribble(
  ~id, ~age, ~visit, ~score,
  1, 34, "baseline", 12,
  1, 34, "followup", 15,
  2, 51, "baseline", 9
)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

**a)** Not tidy. The column headers `1999` and `2000` are *values* of a variable
called `year` (problem 1). Fix with `pivot_longer()`:

```{r}
#| label: ex1-tidy-a
a |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = !country,
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "cases",
    names_transform = list(year = as.integer)
  )
```

**b)** Not tidy. The `rate` column contains two variables, cases and population
(problem 2). Fix with `separate_wider_delim()`:

```{r}
#| label: ex1-tidy-b
b |>
  separate_wider_delim(rate, delim = "/", names = c("cases", "population")) |>
  mutate(across(c(cases, population), as.numeric))
```

**c)** This one is arguable, and that is the point. It is tidy *if* the
observational unit is a visit — one row per visit, each column a property of
that visit. But `age` is a property of the *person*, not the visit, and it is
repeated on every row (problem 4). If a person's age were later corrected, you
would have to change it in several places, and might miss one.

The strict solution is two tables:

```{r}
#| label: ex1-tidy-c
people <- c_data |>
  distinct(id, age)

visits <- c_data |>
  select(id, visit, score)

people
visits
```

In practice a single table is usually more convenient and this level of
normalisation is overkill for a small analysis dataset. Knowing that the
redundancy is there is what matters.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Exercise 2: tidy or clean?

For each problem below, decide whether it is a **tidy** problem (shape) or a
**clean** problem (content), and name the function you would use.

1. Height is recorded as `"165 cm"` rather than `165`.
2. There is one column per week of a 12-week study.
3. The same participant appears twice with identical values.
4. Sex is recorded as `"Woman"`, `"woman"` and `"WOMAN"`.
5. Systolic and diastolic blood pressure are in one column as `"132/85"`.
6. Ten participants have no row for the follow-up visit.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

1. **Clean.** The shape is fine; the value is text where a number belongs.
   `parse_number()`.
2. **Tidy.** Column headers are values of a `week` variable. `pivot_longer()`.
3. **Clean.** `distinct()` — but check first with `janitor::get_dupes()` whether
   the rows really are identical.
4. **Clean.** `str_to_title()`, then `count()` to confirm.
5. **Tidy.** Two variables in one cell. `separate_wider_delim()`.
6. **Tidy**, and consequential. `complete()` makes the missingness explicit so
   it appears in your counts instead of vanishing.

Number 6 is the one most people place in the wrong category. It looks like
missing data — a cleaning problem — but the missingness is invisible precisely
because the *shape* is incomplete. Fix the shape and the cleaning problem
becomes visible.
:::
:::
